look_here_first: PHOTOGRAPH THE BASE before flowers: Texas sage is NOT a true rosette, but has basal leaves plus stem leaves. Basal leaves are narrowly elliptic to oblanceolate (~25–60 × 4–10+ mm); then look for terminal many-flowered raceme with leaflike bracts. Critical tiny confirmation is glandular hairs SUNKEN in pits on the foliage; Engelmann has elevated tack-shaped glands.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Low perennial with both basal and cauline leaves, sunken/pitted glandular hairs, conspicuous bracts, and a sharply pointed strongly ribbed calyx.

project_inclusion.range_basis: UT Hays County flora, Travis County Balcones Canyonlands records, and UT Williamson County treatment; no county presence inferred.

morphology_keys.habit: Taprooted perennial with woody caudex, usually short.
morphology_keys.leaves: Both basal and cauline opposite leaves; basal blades narrow oblanceolate to elliptic.
morphology_keys.surface: Leaf surfaces have sunken/pitted glandular hairs.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Terminal raceme with conspicuous leaflike bracts.
best_field_traits: Joey's Borderlands podcast context places this sage in xeric scrub/limestone-hill country; use habitat as supporting context after checking the ribbed pointed calyx and pitted glandular hairs.
Basal AND cauline leaves (but NOT a true rosette)
Leaflike pointed bracts and many-flowered terminal raceme
Glandular hairs sunken in leaf pits (microscope/macro only)
morphology_keys.joey_field_context: A Borderlands podcast transcript normalizes Joey's spoken taxon to Salvia texana with high confidence and associates it with xeric scrub/limestone hills. The archive still flags an audio check as desirable, so this is kept as attributed habitat context rather than a new diagnostic character.
morphology_keys.basal_rosette_correction: S. texana has BASAL leaves and cauline leaves, but detailed UT Austin specimen treatment explicitly says NOT ROSETTED; do not call the plant a basal rosette.
morphology_keys.basal_leaf_measurement: Basal blade narrowly oblanceolate to narrowly elliptic, ~25–60 × 4–10+ mm, petiolate; cauline leaves sessile and narrower. Width overlaps Engelmann at 4–5 mm.
morphology_keys.flowering_axis: Terminal many-flowered raceme, often 8–14 opposite pairs of flowers with conspicuous sharply pointed leaflike bracts, not paired 3-flowered cymes per node like S. engelmannii.
morphology_keys.calyx_measurement: Green calyx ~11–12 mm long, conspicuously 10-ribbed and sharply pointed; individual pitted glandular hairs need high magnification.
morphology_keys.gland_surface: Sunken glandular hairs lie in pits on foliage/calyx. Tiny structures usually NOT resolved in general-purpose flower photos.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Engelmann sage lacks the basal-leaf set and has conspicuous tack-shaped glands. Azure sage is much taller with a long open flowering axis.

steps.question: Are both basal and stem leaves present?
steps.here: Texas sage: basal leaves plus cauline leaves; base not arranged as a persistent true rosette. Study complete plant, not only a cropped flowering tip.

steps.question: Is basal blade narrowly oblanceolate to elliptic and often 4–10+ mm wide?
steps.here: Texas: ~25–60 mm long; Engelmann stem leaves are linear ~3–5 mm wide. Width overlaps at 4–5 mm.

steps.question: Are blooms arranged as a many-flowered raceme with large pointed leafy bracts?
steps.here: Texas sage often 8–14 opposite pairs of flowers; Engelmann has opposing 3-flowered cymes.

steps.question: Can you see the pointed bracts and 10 ribs?
steps.here: Texas 11–12 mm sharply pointed 10-ribbed calyx; Engelmann also 10-ribbed and short-awned so don't identify from ribs alone.

steps.question: Are the minute glands recessed into shallow pits?
steps.here: Texas: pitted glands; Engelmann raised tack-shaped glands. MUST use actual adequate macro with scale; existing broad photos cannot show this reliably.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: TEXANA: basal + stem leaves, pit glands, pointed bracts. ENGELMANN: stem leaves only, tack glands, three-flower cymes.

mini_glossary.oblanceolate: ob-LAN-see-uh-late — a narrow leaf widest above its middle, near its tip
mini_glossary.bract: BRAKT — a modified leaf just below a flower or flower cluster
mini_glossary.raceme: ray-SEEM — an unbranched flowering axis with individual stalked flowers
mini_glossary.calyx: KAY-liks — the cup of sepals around the flower base
mini_glossary.glandular_hair: Tiny hair with a gland at its tip or embedded in its surface
